claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure characterized by multilevel chemical fluctuations.
A multi-fidelity framework can combine physics-informed surrogate modeling with hierarchical microstructural descriptors.
The proposed framework can predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness of hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed framework will have lower computational cost than traditional CALPHAD and first-principles approaches.
The proposed framework will be more accurate than traditional CALPHAD and first-principles approaches.

Coarse-grained physics simulations and experimentally derived descriptors such as interface chemistry and nanoscale heterogeneity metrics can be integrated to train mechanical-response surrogate models.
The scale and distribution of chemical and microstructural fluctuations mediate local stress distributions.
Multiscale imaging and compositional features, combined with targeted physics simulations, enable an ML model to learn mappings from heterostructural states to tensile and fracture responses.
Targeted physics simulations and surrogate modeling reduce the need for exhaustive first-principles calculations.
Hierarchical microstructural descriptors capture the principal mediators of both tensile and fracture behavior.
The framework is expected to reduce average prediction error by about 20%.
Prediction errors are expected to decrease from approximately 11–20% to approximately 9–16%.
The framework is expected to reduce computational time by approximately a factor of ten.
Support-vector-machine yield-strength predictions for refractory high-entropy alloys have average errors in the approximate 11–20% range over temperatures from 20°C to 800°C.
Existing approaches combine machine learning, CALPHAD, and first-principles calculations for alloy-property prediction.
Existing approaches are computationally intensive when extended to full tensile-property and fracture-toughness prediction.
The framework remains reliable from 20°C to approximately 600°C if the hierarchical heterostructure is preserved and no additional phase separation or extreme degradation occurs.

The method becomes unreliable when microstructural heterogeneity lies substantially outside the training distribution, including after unanticipated phase transformations or extreme nanoscale inhomogeneity.
Above approximately 600°C, additional mechanisms may dominate and make the model unreliable.
